title: Tk 41,090 crore fifth primary education programme approved
excerpt: PEDP-5 runs to June 2031. The World Bank, ADB, EU, UNICEF and UNESCO are expected to fund about a fifth of it, but agreements are not yet signed.

image.alt: A tin-roofed government primary school building in rural Bangladesh
image.credit: Nurunnaby Chowdhury (Hasive) / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC), chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, has approved the fifth Primary Education Development Programme (PEDP-5) at a cost of Tk 41,090.48 crore, The Business Standard reported. The approval came at a meeting on 4 November. Devlens is reporting it now as part of its coverage of new financing for primary education.

What it pays for

  • 15,641 classrooms, including special classrooms in hilly and remote areas and temporary schools where needed.
  • 1,500 sanitation and wash blocks, 10,000 boundary walls, tube wells, other water sources and water quality testing.
  • Multimedia classrooms with interactive panels and internet in 20,000 government primary schools (Tk 1,183.46 crore), and a tablet for each teacher, with training.
  • Uniforms, bags, shoes and socks for pupils from pre-primary to Class V (Tk 10,065.21 crore, about a quarter of the total).
  • A tree-planting scheme for about 10.6 million pupils (Tk 53.09 crore).

Conditions

The Planning Commission asked for a revised proposal within two weeks, a cut to the Tk 436 crore consultancy budget, routine running costs to move to the revenue budget within two years, and faster completion reports for PEDP-3 and PEDP-4, the newspaper reported. State Minister for Planning Zonayed Saki said the prime minister had asked for the programme to be expedited.

Why it matters

PEDP-5 will shape primary schooling for five years. The World Bank’s $300 million credit approved on 6 November supports PEDP-5. The large share for uniforms and equipment, compared with teacher training and learning, is likely to draw questions from education groups, since about half of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, according to the World Bank. NGOs running non-formal, pre-primary and inclusive education should watch how the programme handles out-of-school and hard-to-reach children.

What to watch

  • The revised proposal and whether the consultancy budget is cut.
  • Signing of loan and grant agreements with the partners.
